note: In Athens, the term referred to the portico associated with the archon basileus, an official connected with justice. The word later became the name for a Roman public hall and, eventually, a Christian church type.

meaning: high city / highest part of a city
note: akros means ‘highest’ or ‘upper,’ while polis means ‘city.’
The word developed from the idea of people assembling, and came to mean the public square or marketplace where that assembly took place.
A stoa was a usually detached covered colonnade used for walking, shelter, or conversation. The same word gave us ‘Stoic,’ from the school taught at the Stoa Poikile in Athens.
The name describes the defining arrangement: columns standing around a court, temple, or other space.
In architecture, a hypostyle hall has a roof or ceiling carried by rows of columns.
In classical architecture, naos refers to the temple’s inner chamber. It is the Greek counterpart of the later architectural term ‘cella.’
The Latin word could mean a small room or store-room; in temple architecture it came to denote the enclosed inner room containing the deity’s image.

meaning: the space in front of the temple’s inner sanctuary
note: The name is literally spatial: it identifies the portico or vestibule immediately in front of the naos/cella.
The word originally referred to a dome and came to be used for round buildings, including the beehive-shaped Mycenaean tomb type.
In archaeological usage, dromos is the passage leading into an ancient Egyptian or Mycenaean underground tomb.

meaning: marketplace / open public place / place of assembly
note: The Roman forum was a public open space. The modern sense of a forum as a place for discussion grows from that older idea of public assembly.

meaning: central court / main room of a house
note: The exact deeper origin is debated. Ancient Latin atrium referred to the central court or main room of a house, traditionally associated with the hearth.
The word connects a columned passage to the idea of an entrance or gateway.
The English architectural sense was borrowed from Greek pylon, ‘gateway,’ for the monumental gateways of Egyptian temples.
The Greek word obeliskos was a diminutive of obelos, a spit or pointed pillar. The pointed shape helped motivate the comparison.
In Egyptian archaeology, serdab became the name for the small chamber associated with a mastaba and the statue of the deceased.
The Akkadian word is linked to a root meaning ‘to build high,’ fitting the stepped, elevated form of a ziggurat.
Greek authors associated sphinx with sphingein, ‘to squeeze/bind,’ but the true origin of the name is uncertain and may reflect an Egyptian term instead.
The later Arabic architectural word refers to a bench or raised platform, a visual comparison often used to explain the English archaeological term for the flat-roofed tomb.
